modules.title: Meaning, Definition, and Scope of Economics
text: Economics is a social science that studies how individuals, businesses, and societies make choices when resources are limited.
Human wants are unlimited, while resources like land, labour, capital, and time are scarce (limited). Economics explains how to use these scarce resources efficiently to satisfy maximum wants.
The word 'Economics' comes from the Greek word 'Oikonomia', meaning household management.
Adam Smith (a Scottish thinker) is widely known as the Father of Economics, though he was influenced by the French Physiocrats.

Basic Economic Questions (Central Problems of an Economy)
Because resources are scarce and human wants are unlimited, every society must answer three central questions:
Basic Economic Questions (Central Problems of an Economy)

What to Produce? (Problem of Allocation):; Deciding which goods to make and in what quantities—for example, consumption goods vs capital goods, civil goods vs military goods, and necessity goods vs luxury goods.; Making more of one good means making less of another because resources are limited.
Basic Economic Questions (Central Problems of an Economy)

How to Produce? (Problem of Choice of Technique):; Deciding which production method to use—for example, cotton cloth using handlooms vs power looms, or wheat using manual farming vs modern machinery.; Labour-Intensive Technique: Uses more labour relative to capital (e.g., handlooms, manual farming). Best where labour is abundant.; Capital-Intensive Technique: Uses more capital/machinery relative to labour (e.g., power looms, automated machinery). Best where capital is abundant.; Choice depends on the availability of resources and their relative prices.
Basic Economic Questions (Central Problems of an Economy)

For Whom to Produce? (Problem of Distribution):; Deciding how total national output is shared among members of society (e.g., mainly for a few rich people or for the large population).; A society aiming to benefit the maximum people produces necessities for everyone first, and luxury goods later.

modules.title: Basic Concepts in Economics
text: Goods: Tangible physical items that can be seen, touched, and stored (e.g., food, clothing, machinery).
Services: Intangible activities performed for consumers that have no physical form (e.g., education, healthcare, transportation, banking).
Both goods and services satisfy human wants and raise living standards.

By Availability and Scarcity:; Free Goods: Available in abundant supply at zero price; no scarcity and no market price (e.g., sunlight, air, natural wind).; Economic Goods: Scarce compared to human wants; involve a production cost and have a market price (e.g., food, clothing, vehicles, electronics).

By Stage of Use:; Intermediate Goods: Used as inputs to make other goods, not for direct consumption; they get transformed or used up in production (e.g., cotton used to make cloth, steel used to make machines).; Final Goods: Ready for direct consumption by consumers; need no further processing and are counted when measuring total economic output (e.g., clothes, furniture, consumer electronics).
Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour
Normal Goods - How Demand Behaves: Demand increases when consumer income increases; Examples: Branded clothing, household appliances, better-quality food.
Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour
Inferior Goods - How Demand Behaves: Demand decreases when consumer income increases (consumers switch to better alternatives); Examples: Low-cost food items, basic- quality products.
Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour
Substitute Goods - How Demand Behaves: Goods that can replace each other; if the price of one rises, demand for the other rises; Examples: Tea and coffee.
Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour
Complementary Goods - How Demand Behaves: Goods used together; if the price of one rises, demand for the other falls; Examples: Cars and fuel.
Utility is the satisfaction or pleasure a consumer gets from consuming a good or service.
Utility is subjective (the same product gives different satisfaction to different people) and relative (satisfaction changes with time, place, and ownership).
Form Utility - How It Is Created: Converting raw materials into finished goods through production; Example: Cotton transformed into cloth, and cloth into garments.
Time Utility - How It Is Created: Storing goods so they are available at the exact time consumers need them most; Example: Cold drinks in hot summer weather; seasonal clothing.
Place Utility - How It Is Created: Transporting and distributing goods from surplus areas to locations where demand exists; Example: Moving agricultural produce from rural farms to urban markets.
Possession Utility - How It Is Created: Transferring ownership of a good from seller to consumer through market exchange; Example: Buying a product in a market so you own and can use it.

modules.title: Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics
text: The terms microeconomics and macroeconomics were coined by Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch in 1933.
Both branches are closely connected: understanding the whole economy requires understanding individual choices, and individual choices are affected by the overall economy.
Derived from the Greek word 'mikros' (meaning small).
Studies small individual economic units—such as an individual consumer, household, firm, or industry—and how they allocate scarce resources.
Gardner Ackley: Microeconomics deals with dividing total output among industries, products, and firms, allocating resources among competing groups, income distribution, and relative prices.
Maurice Dobb: Microeconomics is a "microscopic study of the economy"—like looking at the economy through a microscope.
Product Pricing: How prices of individual goods are set by demand (consumer choice) and supply (producer decisions).
Factor Pricing Theory: Determining rewards for factors of production—Land (Rent), Labour (Wages), Capital (Interest), and Entrepreneurship (Profit).
Theory of Economic Welfare: Studying efficiency in production, consumption, and distribution to maximise public welfare.
Analyses individual consumer and producer behaviour.
Helps the government frame price policies, economic development plans, and taxation structures.
Explains international trade gains, tariffs, Balance of Payments (BOP), and exchange rates.
Suggests ways to reduce waste and improve social welfare.
Unrealistic assumptions: Assumes full employment and laissez-faire/no government intervention.
Narrow picture: Looks at isolated parts, not the whole economy.
Misleading results: What is true for one individual may not be true for the whole economy.
Abstract nature: Lacks full real-world applicability.
Limited guidance: Provides minimal utility for macro-level national policymaking.
Studies the behaviour and performance of the entire economy as a whole using aggregate (combined) variables.
Core Aggregate Variables: National Income, Employment, Inflation, Total Output, Aggregate Demand, Aggregate Supply, total savings, general price level, and overall consumption.
Main Concerns: Determining national income and employment, achieving full employment of resources, maintaining economic stability, tackling inflation and unemployment, and promoting economic growth.
Main Analytical Tools: Aggregate Demand (total demand for goods and services) and Aggregate Supply (total output produced); Equilibrium occurs where total demand equals total supply.
Unit of Study - Microeconomics: Individual economic units (households, firms, industries); Macroeconomics: The entire economy and overall economic aggregates.
Main Concern - Microeconomics: Price determination and efficient allocation of resources; Macroeconomics: National income, employment, inflation, and overall economic performance.
Analytical Tools - Microeconomics: Demand and supply of individual goods and services; Macroeconomics: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply of the whole economy.
Equilibrium Focus - Microeconomics: Equilibrium of individual consumers, producers, or markets; Macroeconomics: Overall economic equilibrium involving total income and employment.

Examples of Variables - Microeconomics: Individual income, individual consumption, price of a specific good (e.g., fish), output of a firm; Macroeconomics: National income (GDP), general price level, inflation rate, national unemployment, total output.

Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics

Positive Economics ("What is"):; Objective, scientific, fact-based explanations of how the economy actually works—no personal opinions or value judgements.; Statements can be tested, proved, or disproved using data (even a false factual claim like "the moon is made of cheese" is positive because it can be empirically tested).; Examples: "An increase in taxes raises the price of goods"; "Higher interest rates reduce borrowing"; "The retired population of Mexico has increased over the last 15 years"; "High mortgage interest rates encourage saving.".

modules.title: Introduction to Economics
text: Economics is a social science that studies how individuals and societies make choices in the presence of limited resources. Since human wants are unlimited and resources such as land, labour, capital, and time are scarce, every society faces the problem of selection and allocation. Economics helps in understanding how these scarce resources are utilized efficiently to satisfy maximum wants. It explains not only the production of goods and services but also their distribution and consumption for promoting human welfare. The subject of economics begins with understanding its meaning, nature, objectives, and scope. It examines how economic activities are organized and how decisions are made regarding what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. These central problems arise because resources are limited in relation to wants. Economics therefore provides a systematic framework to analyse decision-making at both the individual and societal levels.

The study of economics is broadly divided into two major branches: microeconomics and macroeconomics. Microeconomics focuses on individual economic units such as households and firms. It studies price determination, demand and supply, and the allocation of resources in specific markets. Macroeconomics, on the other hand, examines the economy. It deals with aggregate variables such as national income, employment, inflation, and overall economic growth. Both branches are interrelated and together provide a complete understanding of economic functioning.

This units, also introduces the basic concepts of goods and services, their types, and the concept of utility. Goods may be free or economic, consumer or producer, normal or inferior, and substitutes or complements. Utility refers to the satisfaction derived from the consumption of goods and services. Understanding these concepts is essential for analysing consumer behaviour and market operations. In addition, the units explain the methods of economic analysis. Economists use inductive reasoning, which moves from specific facts to general theories, and deductive reasoning, which moves from general assumptions to specific conclusions. It also distinguishes between positive economics, which is based on facts and objective analysis, and normative economics, which involves value judgments about what ought to be.
Overall, this units lays the foundation for the systematic study of economics by introducing its key concepts, branches, methods, and perspectives.

Economics is an integral part of our daily life. The word Economics is derived from the Greek term “Oikonomia,” meaning household management. The Scottish thinker Adam Smith, widely regarded as the Father of Economics, laid the foundation of the subject, though he was influenced by the French Physiocrats. There has long been debate among economists regarding the nature of economics—whether it is a science or an art, and if a science, whether positive or normative. Science refers to a systematized body of knowledge verified through observation and experimentation, showing cause-and-effect relationships with universally accepted laws.
As the figure highlights, economics carries both a scientific and an artistic character, each of which is examined below.
Nature of Economics: Economics as a Science

Many economists such as Robbins and Robertson argued that economics possesses scientific characteristics. Economic theories and facts, both micro and macro, are systematically collected and analysed. Laws like demand and supply establish cause-and- effect relationships—for example, price changes affect quantity demanded. Economic laws such as the law of diminishing marginal utility are widely accepted. Economics also uses real-world experiments, such as mixed economic systems combining capitalism and socialism.
Nature of Economics: Economics as a Science

A key issue is whether economics is positive or normative science. Positive economics deals with “what is, what was, and what will be,” focusing on facts and explanations without value judgments. Economists like Senior and Robbins supported this view. Normative economics, on the other hand, deals with “what ought to be” and suggests solutions to economic problems. Thinkers like Pigou and Marshall believed economics cannot be separated from ethics. Hence, economics is both positive and normative.
Nature of Economics: Economics as an Art

Art refers to the practical application of knowledge to solve problems. Economics guides solutions to real issues like unemployment, inflation, and population growth. As T.K. Mehta said, “Knowledge is science, action is art.” Thus, economics is scientific in method and artistic in application.
Nature of Economics: Economics as an Art

At its core, economics seeks to explain how individuals, institutions, and societies identify, organize, and allocate their limited resources in order to satisfy their diverse and expanding needs. It addresses fundamental questions such as what goods and services should be produced, how they should be produced, and who should benefit from them. These questions arise because resources such as land, labour, capital, and technology are finite, while human desires are virtually limitless. Economics provides a structured approach to understanding how societies manage this imbalance between unlimited wants and limited means. By studying economics, individuals gain insights into how economic systems function, how decisions are made at different levels, and how these decisions influence overall well-being and development. Thus, economics serves as an essential tool for understanding both everyday choices and large-scale economic phenomena.

The study of economics aims to provide individuals with the knowledge and analytical skills needed to understand how modern economies function. It helps learners understand the basic principles of economics and how different parts of the economy interact. Economics explains how scarce resources are used efficiently to produce goods and services that satisfy human needs, which is essential in a world of limited resources. Another objective is to familiarize learners with methods of economic analysis, including logical reasoning and the study of real-world data. These methods help in understanding economic behaviour, analysing problems, and making informed decisions. Economics also helps individuals understand different economic systems such as capitalist, socialist, and mixed economies, and how they allocate resources and organize production.
These objectives, summarised above, together explain why the study of economics is valuable.

In addition, economics explains the basic economic problems of what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. It also examines the role of key decision-making units such as households, firms, and governments, and how their interactions influence the overall economy. Overall, the study of economics helps individuals understand economic processes and make better personal, professional, and policy-related decisions.

Defining economics has been a subject of debate among economists for many years, and no single definition has gained universal acceptance. Different economists have emphasized different aspects of economic activity depending on their perspectives and the historical context in which they worked. As a result, several major approaches to defining economics have emerged, each highlighting a particular dimension of the subject. They are, The timeline above traces how the definition of economics evolved across four major phases, detailed below.

The wealth definition is one of the earliest interpretations of economics and was strongly associated with Adam Smith. According to this perspective, economics is primarily concerned with the production, accumulation, and distribution of material wealth. It focuses on how individuals and nations acquire wealth and how economic activities contribute to increasing national prosperity. Wealth, in this sense, refers to tangible goods and resources that have monetary value. This definition emphasizes economic growth, trade, and production as central components of economic study. However, it has been criticized for giving excessive importance to wealth while neglecting human welfare, social well-being, and non-material aspects of life. Critics argue that wealth alone does not guarantee happiness or social progress, and therefore economics should not be limited only to the study of material wealth.

The welfare definition of economics was developed to address the limitations of the wealth definition. This approach, associated with economists such as Alfred Marshall, views economics as a study of human welfare rather than merely the accumulation of wealth. According to this definition, economics examines how economic activities affect the well-being and quality of life of individuals and society. Wealth is considered important, but only to improve human welfare. This perspective emphasizes the role of economic activities in promoting happiness, reducing poverty, and improving living standards. It highlights that the ultimate objective of economic activity is to enhance human well-being rather than simply increase material possessions. However, this definition has also faced criticism because welfare is subjective and difficult to measure accurately, making it challenging to analyse in precise economic terms.

The scarcity definition is one of the most widely accepted and influential definitions in modern economics. It was proposed by Lionel Robbins, who defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour in relation to unlimited wants and scarce resources that have alternative uses. This definition highlights the fundamental problem of scarcity, which arises because resources such as land, labour, and capital are limited, while human desires are unlimited. As a result, individuals and societies must make choices about how to allocate resources efficiently among competing needs. This definition emphasizes decision-making, choice, and the concept of opportunity cost, which refers to the value of the next best alternative that is sacrificed when a choice is made. The scarcity definition is widely appreciated because it applies to all economic situations and clearly explains the core problem that economics seeks to address.

The growth definition of economics focuses on the expansion of an economy’s productive capacity and the improvement of living standards over time. This perspective is closely associated with modern economists such as Paul Samuelson, who emphasized the importance of economic growth, development, and efficient resource utilization. According to this definition, economics studies how societies use resources to produce goods and services and how they improve their productive capabilities through technological progress, capital formation, and innovation. This definition is particularly relevant in the context of developing countries, where economic growth plays a crucial role in reducing poverty, creating employment opportunities, and improving overall welfare. It highlights the dynamic nature of economics and its role in promoting long- term development and sustainability.
Taken together, these four approaches show how the focus of economics shifted from wealth to growth over time.

The scope of economics has expanded considerably over time, reflecting the increasing complexity of modern societies and economies. Economics is no longer limited to the study of wealth and production but now includes the analysis of resource allocation, human welfare, economic development, and environmental sustainability. It examines how individuals, firms, and governments make decisions regarding the use of scarce resources and how these decisions affect economic efficiency, growth, and social well- being. As economic systems evolve, economics continues to incorporate new areas of study to address emerging challenges and changing societal needs.
As shown above, the scope of economics extends across several specialised branches, discussed in the paragraphs that follow.

One important branch within the scope of economics is development economics, which focuses on improving the economic conditions of developing countries. It examines issues such as poverty, unemployment, income inequality, and economic growth, and explores ways to enhance living standards through better use of resources and effective policies. Industrial economics studies the functioning and organization of industries and the behaviour of firms in different market conditions. It helps in understanding production decisions, competition, pricing, and the role of industries in economic progress.

Transport economics deals with the economic aspects of transportation systems and their role in facilitating trade and mobility. It examines the efficient use of transport resources, the cost and benefits of transport infrastructure, and the importance of transport in supporting economic activities. Welfare economics focuses on the well-being of individuals and society. It studies how economic activities and government policies affect social welfare, resource distribution, and economic fairness. Environmental economics examines the relationship between economic activities and the environment. It emphasizes the need to use natural resources responsibly and develop policies that promote sustainable development while minimizing environmental damage.

Despite the expansion into many specialized areas, the core of economic analysis is based on its two main branches: microeconomics and macroeconomics. Microeconomics studies the behaviour of individual economic units such as households, firms, and industries. It examines how these units make decisions regarding consumption, production, and pricing, and how they interact in markets. Macroeconomics studies the overall functioning of the economy, including national income, employment, inflation, and economic growth.

Thus, the scope of economics is wide and continuously growing. It includes the study of various sectors, economic systems, and policies that influence economic development and human welfare. Economics helps in understanding real-world economic problems and provides a framework for making informed decisions to promote efficient resource use and improve the overall well-being of society.

Economic problems faced by an economic system due to the scarcity of resources are known as basic economic problems. These problems are common to all economic systems and are also called the central problems of an economy. Therefore, every human society must answer the following three basic questions:
Each of the three central questions illustrated above is examined in turn below.

This problem is also known as the problem of allocation of resources. It implies that every economy must decide which goods are to be produced and in what quantities. The economy has to make choices such as:

Necessity goods versus luxury goods Since economic resources are limited, the production of one type of good must be reduced if more of another type is to be produced. Generally, the final choice of any economy is a combination of various types of goods, but the exact nature of this combination depends upon the specific circumstances and objectives of the economy. ii. How to Produce? This problem is also known as the problem of choice of technique. Once an economy decides the types of goods to be produced and their quantities, it must determine the method or technique of production.
Cotton cloth can be produced using handlooms, power looms, or automatic looms.
Wheat can be cultivated using primitive tools and manual labour, or modern machinery with less labour. Broadly, production techniques are classified into two groups:
Labour-intensive techniques: Use more labour relative to capital per unit of output.

Capital-intensive techniques: Use more capital relative to labour per unit of output. The comparison above clarifies the trade-off that guides the choice of production technique described next. The choice between these techniques depends on the availability of factors of production and their relative prices. Making the right choice ensures the best possible use of limited resources to maximize output. iii. For Whom to Produce? This problem is also known as the problem of distribution of national product. It relates to how the total output produced in an economy is distributed among members of society. The economy must decide, for instance, whether goods should be produced mainly for a small number of rich people or for the large population of poor people. An economy that aims to benefit the maximum number of people will first prioritize the production of necessities for the entire population and then move towards the production of luxury goods.

An economic system refers to the set of organizational and institutional arrangements through which a society allocates resources and answers the three basic economic questions: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce. It determines ownership of resources, decision-making authority, and the role of government in economic activities. Generally economic systems are classified into three types:
The three systems shown above differ chiefly in who owns and controls the means of production, as explained below.

i. Capitalist Economy (Free Market Economy) A capitalist economy is the oldest formal economic system, which became widespread in the mid-19th century. In this system, the means of production are privately owned, and production is carried out by private entrepreneurs mainly for profit, with minimal government intervention.
Presence of negative externalities (e.g., pollution) Advantages:
Growth in income and living standards.

Environmental and social costs (negative externalities) ii. Command Economy (Socialist Economy) In a command economy, all means of production are owned and controlled by the state. Economic decisions regarding production, distribution, and pricing are made through central planning with the objective of maximizing social welfare.
Reduction of monopolies and inequalities Disadvantages:
Slower economic growth iii. Mixed Economy A mixed economy combines features of both capitalism and socialism. Public and private sectors coexist, sharing responsibility for economic development.
Co-existence of public and private sectors.
Benefits of private property and profit motive.
Risk of corruption and black markets Positioned along the spectrum above, the mixed economy blends the market and command approaches just described.

Economic activity primarily aims at producing goods and services to fulfil human needs and wants. Goods are tangible items that have a physical form and can be seen, touched, and stored. They directly satisfy human wants, such as food, clothing, and machinery. Services, in contrast, are intangible and do not have a physical presence. They provide satisfaction through activities performed for consumers, such as education, healthcare, transportation, and banking. Both goods and services are essential because they contribute to improving living standards and supporting the functioning of the economy.
Goods and Services: Classification of Goods

Economics classifies resources and goods based on their availability and their ability to satisfy human wants. This classification helps in understanding scarcity, production, and consumption in an economy.
Goods and Services: Classification of Goods
The classification shown above is explained through the two contrasting pairs described below.
Goods and Services: Free good V/S Economic good

Free goods are those that are available in abundant supply and do not require payment for their use. Their availability is greater than the demand at a zero price, so they do not involve scarcity. Examples include sunlight, air, and natural wind. Since these goods are freely available, they do not have a market price and do not require careful allocation.
Goods and Services: Free good V/S Economic good

Economic goods are those that are limited in supply in relation to human wants. Because they are scarce, they have value and must be used carefully and efficiently. These goods usually involve a cost of production and are bought and sold in markets. Examples include food, clothing, vehicles, and electronic products. Scarcity makes it necessary for individuals and societies to make choices regarding their use.
Goods and Services: Intermediate V/S Final good

Intermediate goods are goods that are used in the production of other goods and services. They are not meant for direct consumption but serve as inputs in the production process. These goods are either transformed or used up during production. Examples include raw materials like cotton used to produce cloth or steel used to manufacture machines.
Goods and Services: Intermediate V/S Final good

Final goods are those goods that are ready for consumption and are used to directly satisfy human wants. They do not require further processing and represent the end result of production. Examples include clothes, furniture, and consumer electronics. Final goods are important because they reflect the actual output available for consumers and are used in measuring the overall production of an economy.
Goods and Services: Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour

Goods can also be classified based on how their demand changes with variations in income and the prices of related goods. This classification helps in understanding consumer preferences and market demand.
Goods and Services: Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour

Normal Goods: Normal goods are goods for which demand increases as consumer income increases; When people earn more, they tend to purchase more of these goods because they can afford better quality or greater quantity; Examples include branded clothing, household appliances, and better-quality food.
Goods and Services: Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour

Inferior Goods: Inferior goods are goods for which demand decreases as consumer income increases; These goods are usually lower-cost alternatives that consumers prefer when their income is limited; As income rises, consumers shift to superior alternatives; Examples include low-cost food items or basic quality products.
Goods and Services: Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour

Substitute Goods: Substitute goods are goods that can replace each other in satisfying the same need; When the price of one good increases, consumers tend to switch to its substitute, increasing its demand; For example, tea and coffee are substitutes because consumers may choose one instead of the other.
Goods and Services: Types of Goods Based on Consumer Behaviour

Complementary Goods: Complementary goods are goods that are used together to satisfy a particular want. The demand for one good depends on the demand for the other. For example, cars and fuel are complementary goods because fuel is necessary for using a car. If the price of one complementary good increase, the demand for the related good decrease. The figure summarises how the demand for each type of good responds to changes in income and related prices.

Utility refers to the satisfaction or pleasure that a consumer obtains from consuming goods or services. It is a consumer-centred concept and varies from person to person based on individual preferences, needs, and circumstances. Utility is subjective in nature, meaning that the same product may provide different levels of satisfaction to different individuals. It is also relative, as the satisfaction derived from a good can change depending on factors such as time, place, and ownership. Utility can be classified into different types based on how it is created and experienced by consumers.

Form Utility: Form utility is created when raw materials are converted into finished goods that are more useful and capable of satisfying human wants. Raw materials in their natural state often provide limited satisfaction, but when they undergo production and transformation, their usefulness increases significantly. This transformation adds value and enhances the ability of the product to meet consumer needs. The process of production involves combining factors such as land, labour, and capital to create goods in a form that is suitable for consumption. For example, cotton is transformed into cloth, and cloth is further made into garments, which provide greater satisfaction to consumers. Thus, form utility is generated by changing the physical form of resources into finished products that better fulfil human wants.

Time Utility: Time utility refers to the satisfaction that a consumer derives from a good depending on the time at which it is available or consumed. The usefulness of a product is always not the same, and it may provide greater satisfaction when it is available at the right moment. For example, a cold drink provides more satisfaction during hot weather than during cold weather. Similarly, certain goods such as seasonal clothing or agricultural products provide higher utility during specific periods. Time utility is created by storing goods and making them available when consumers need them most. This ensures that goods are supplied at the appropriate time to maximize satisfaction.

Place Utility: Place utility arises when goods are made available at locations where consumers need them. A product may have little or no utility in one place but may provide significant satisfaction in another location where demand exists. Transporting goods from areas of surplus to areas of shortage increases their usefulness and value. For example, agricultural products grown in rural areas gain greater utility when it is transported to urban markets where consumers can purchase and use it. Place utility is therefore created through transportation and distribution, which ensure that goods reach the right place where they are most useful.

Possession Utility: Possession utility refers to the satisfaction that consumers gain when they acquire ownership of a good or service. This type of utility is created through the process of exchange in the market, where consumers purchase goods to satisfy their needs and wants. A product provides real satisfaction only when it is owned and used by the consumer. Markets facilitate this transfer of ownership, allowing consumers to choose goods according to their preferences and purchasing power. Consumers select combinations of goods that they believe will provide them with the highest level of satisfaction. Thus, possession utility is created when goods are transferred from producers or sellers to consumers, enabling them to use and benefit from those goods. Each form of utility shown above adds value in a distinct way, as outlined in the points listed earlier.

Economics is studied at two main levels: microeconomics and macroeconomics. These two branches focus on different aspects of economic activity but are closely interconnected and support each other. Microeconomics examines the behaviour of individual economic units, while macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. A proper understanding of the overall economy requires knowledge of individual decision- making, and similarly, individual economic behaviour is influenced by broader economic conditions. Together, these two branches provide a complete understanding of how economic systems function, how resources are allocated, and how economic stability and growth are achieved.

The terms microeconomics and macroeconomics were coined by the Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch in 1933. The word micro is derived from the Greek word mikros, meaning small. When economic problems are studied with reference to small economic units such as an individual consumer or an individual producer, it is called microeconomics. The basic economic problem is the problem of choice relating to the allocation of scarce resources to alternative uses at the individual level (both consumer and producer).

As Gardner Ackley states, “Microeconomics deals with the division of total output among industries, products and firms and the allocation of resources among competing groups. It considers problems of income distribution. Its interest is in relative prices of goods and services.” According to Maurice Dobb, microeconomics is a microscopic study of the economy. It is like looking at the economy through a microscope to understand the working of markets for individual commodities and the behaviour of individual consumers and producers.
Building on this focus, the scope, importance and limitations of microeconomics are set out below.
The scope or subject matter of microeconomics includes:

1. Product Pricing: The price of an individual commodity is determined by market forces of demand and supply. Consumer choice and allocation of income are studied under the theory of demand, while producers’ decisions regarding output and input combination come under the theory of supply.

2. Factor Pricing Theory: Microeconomics determines factor prices for land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship in the form of rent, wages, interest, and profit respectively. These are the factors contributing to production.
Individual Behaviour Analysis: Studies consumer and producer behaviour in decision-making.
Resource Allocation: Helps in efficient use of scarce resources.
Tool for Economic Policies: Assists the state in price policy formulation.
Economic Planning: Aids in economic development policies.
Taxation Decisions: Helps government fix tax rates and structure.
International Trade: Explains trade gains, tariffs, BOP issues, and exchange rates.
Social Welfare: Suggests ways to reduce wastage and improve welfare under different market structures.
Unrealistic Assumptions: Assumes full employment and laissez-faire conditions.
Narrow Picture: Studies parts, not the whole economy.
Misleading Results: Individual behaviour cannot represent the entire economy.
Abstract Nature: Lacks full real-world applicability.
Limited Policy Guidance: Offers less practical help in macro-level policymaking.

Macroeconomics studies the behaviour and performance of the economy. Instead of focusing on individual units, it examines aggregate economic variables that reflect the overall condition of the economy. This branch analyses broad economic issues such as national income, employment levels, inflation, and overall production. It helps in understanding how the economy grows, how economic stability is maintained, and how economic problems such as unemployment and inflation are addressed. One of the main concerns of macroeconomics is determining the level of national income and employment. It examines how total output and total employment are determined and how they change over time. Macroeconomics also focuses on achieving full employment of resources, ensuring that labour, capital, and other resources are used efficiently. The main analytical tools used in macroeconomics are aggregate demand and aggregate supply, which represent the total demand for goods and services, and the total output produced in the economy. Macroeconomics studies how equilibrium is achieved at the overall level, where total demand equals total supply. Examples of macroeconomic variables include national income, total savings in the economy, the general price level, inflation rate, total production, and overall consumption. This branch helps governments and policymakers design policies to promote economic growth and stability.
As the figure shows, macroeconomics aggregates individual activity into economy-wide measures.

The main aim of economics is to develop reliable generalizations or theories that explain human behaviour in relation to scarce resources. These theories simplify complex real- world situations and help economists understand, predict, and analyse economic activities. To build such theories, economists rely on systematic methods of reasoning and adopt different perspectives while interpreting economic information. Broadly, economic analysis is carried out through logical methods of reasoning and through two major perspectives—positive and normative economics.
Methods of Logical Reasoning: Inductive and Deductive
Economic theories are developed using two principal logical approaches: inductive reasoning and deductive reasoning. Both methods are important and are often used together in economic analysis.
Methods of Logical Reasoning: Inductive and Deductive: Inductive Reasoning

Inductive reasoning is a method in which general conclusions are drawn from specific observations. In this approach, economists begin by collecting detailed facts and data related to a particular problem. After organizing and analysing this information, they identify patterns and relationships among economic variables. From these repeated observations, they formulate general principles or theories. Thus, the direction of reasoning moves from specific facts to broader generalizations. The inductive method usually involves selecting a problem for study, gathering and classifying relevant data, examining the information carefully, and finally establishing cause-and-effect relationships. This method is practical and fact-based, as it builds theories directly from real-world observations.
Methods of Logical Reasoning: Inductive and Deductive: Inductive Reasoning
The upward flow shown above captures how inductive reasoning builds general theories from observed facts.
Methods of Logical Reasoning: Inductive and Deductive: Deductive Reasoning

Deductive reasoning works in the opposite direction. It begins with general assumptions or accepted truths and then applies logical reasoning to reach specific conclusions. In this method, economists start with certain basic assumptions about human behaviour or economic conditions. Based on these assumptions, they develop hypotheses and then test whether these conclusions are valid in real-life situations. The deductive method follows a sequence of identifying the problem, stating assumptions clearly, formulating hypotheses, and verifying them with actual data. Here, reasoning moves from general statements to specific conclusions. This method emphasizes logical consistency and systematic thinking in the development of economic theories.
Methods of Logical Reasoning: Inductive and Deductive: Deductive Reasoning
In contrast, the downward flow above shows how deductive reasoning derives specific conclusions from general premises.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Positive and normative economics are the two fundamental branches of economic analysis, each serving a distinct but complementary role in understanding and guiding economic activity.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics

Positive economics is concerned with objective, scientific, and fact-based explanations of how an economy actually functions. It examines relationships between economic variables such as production, consumption, pricing, taxation, income distribution, and market behaviour without involving personal opinions or value judgements. Its primary aims are to explain economic phenomena and to predict how the economy will respond to policy changes or external shocks. For instance, statements such as “an increase in taxes raises the price of goods” or “higher interest rates reduce borrowing” are positive because they are testable through data and empirical research. In this sense, positive economics resembles natural sciences, relying on observation, hypothesis testing, and evidence.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
These are statements of fact, or at least of a provable nature. Some examples of positive economics:
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
The retired population of Mexico has increased over the last 15 years.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
The Nigerian balance of payments deteriorated last month.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
The moon is made of cheese.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
High mortgage interest rates encourage saving.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics

More African nations will qualify for the World Cup next time. Normative economics, in contrast, deals with prescriptions, recommendations, and value-based judgements about what the economy ought to be like. It addresses questions of welfare, equity, justice, and policy desirability, such as whether governments should reduce inequality, subsidise healthcare, or prioritise environmental protection over industrial growth. Such statements cannot be scientifically proven right or wrong because they depend on ethical beliefs, political ideology, and societal priorities. Many economic propositions combine both elements; for example, stating that the elderly have higher medical expenses is positive, while arguing that the government should subsidise their healthcare is normative. While economics cannot resolve normative disagreements, positive analysis plays a crucial role in informing them by outlining the consequences, costs, and trade-offs of alternative policy choices. Therefore, a clear distinction between positive and normative economics is essential for objective research, rational policy formulation, and meaningful economic debate. Normative statements, or value judgements as they are sometimes called, are matters of opinion or statements of value. They cannot be tested or proven. Some examples:
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
University students should be funded from a new, higher rate of income tax.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Nobody should have to pay for hospital treatment.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Mobile phones should be banned in all public places.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Girls should be given higher university loans than boys.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
The present level of income tax is unfair.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
Acts of terror by the state cannot be justified.
Perspectives of Analysis: Positive and Normative Economics
